title: Waller sets out a December hike preference and a test for going further
summary: Before the October consumer price release, Governor Christopher Waller favoured a 25-basis-point December increase even if monthly inflation improved. A third reading near 0.3 percent or higher for monthly core CPI would lead him to consider 50 basis points. He explained that he had supported October’s hold because communication about the future path had already tightened financial conditions. In his view, consecutive moves were unnecessary, but failing to deliver within a reasonable period could undo the tightening as markets revised their expectations. This was Waller’s own contingent preference, not a December vote or a report of the October CPI outcome.

His inflation analysis focused on how many prices were rising quickly and which components were doing so. September PCE inflation was 0.5 percent for the month and 3.7 percent over twelve months. Core PCE rose 0.3 and 3.1 percent over the same intervals. Waller placed less weight on earlier pressure in prices that statisticians must impute and more on increases in goods and market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of core PCE services components had twelve-month increases above 3 percent. That is a share of components, not the share of household expenditure exposed to those increases.

He identified two possible sources of persistence. A high-tech input-price measure based on purchasing managers’ reports rose in December 2025 and January 2026, ahead of higher producer prices in February. The October survey again suggested possible increases; Waller treated the connection to eventual consumer prices as an inference. Separately, research cited in the speech suggested that energy costs might pass into core prices for longer than before the pandemic. Waller cited reports that insurance and transfers between vessels were adding $20–30 per barrel to oil costs. This was a reported logistics cost, separate from a futures price. He expected limited refining capacity to keep delivered diesel expensive even if crude retreated. The energy study suggested effects on core prices could persist well into 2027 if oil stayed elevated. Both energy and AI-related inputs could contribute at once; the speech did not quantify their separate contributions.

On activity, Waller cited the initial 3.4 percent third-quarter real GDP growth estimate. October payrolls rose by 165,000, previous months were revised upward by 85,000 in total, and unemployment was 4.1 percent. Both six- and twelve-month average payroll gains were nearer 80,000. Under these conditions he judged the level of employment close to maximum, supporting his near-term focus on prices. Strong consumer spending and high-tech investment had supported third-quarter output. Waller expected growth to ease in the current quarter as spending came closer to what household income and wealth could sustain.

His longer-run labour diagnosis was less settled. September’s net gain of 60,000 jobs sat alongside more than five million hires and more than five million separations. Figures 1 and 2 and their accessible JOLTS tables put the September 2026 hiring and separation rates at 3.4 and 3.3 percent of nonfarm employment, respectively, down from 3.9 and 3.8 percent in September 2019. The latter series covers quits as well as layoffs. Low turnover can reflect a population with more older or highly educated workers, improved matches from earlier job switching, or barriers preventing workers from reaching higher-productivity firms. These explanations imply different potential output paths. Waller cited longer unemployment spells and difficulties facing new entrants as reasons to investigate the last possibility. He also cited Beige Book reports of uncertainty delaying hiring, including firms assessing how AI might change their staffing. Footnote 4 reports that the three-month average share unemployed for at least 27 weeks rose from around 18% at the end of 2022 to over 27% through September 2026. The share accounted for by new entrants was near a twenty-year high. Workers typically switched again after a median of three years, leaving open whether pandemic-era switchers had found better matches or were simply approaching another move. He left the causes open.

The prepared remarks were scheduled for 4:00 a.m. EST, or 9:00 a.m. in London. The US October CPI release was still hours away. Measuring a daily change in yields would combine the announcement of his conditional preference with separate news about whether the condition had been met. The remarks describe tightening already priced, without reporting the market-implied odds of either size of December move.

questions.question: Was the December alternative already priced before the speech?
questions.detail: Compare contracts settling around the December meeting and options on those rates immediately before and after the speech, stopping the first window before CPI. Then examine the separate price-release window. A change in the odds of a larger move may alter the shape of the distribution more than its average. Use the Fed’s delivery time and the official statistical release calendar to keep the two events separate.

questions.question: Did broad services inflation signal persistence or a base effect?
questions.detail: Reconstruct Waller’s count of components above 3 percent using unchanged definitions, then compare expenditure-weighted breadth, shorter annualised changes and measures excluding imputed prices. A twelve-month count can stay high after near-term momentum has slowed. BEA detailed PCE tables and the associated expenditure weights would allow both calculations.

questions.question: Does reduced labour turnover indicate better matches or barriers to mobility?
questions.detail: Estimate hiring, separations, wage gains after job changes and unemployment duration by age, education and tenure. Stable jobs with stronger productivity and pay would support the match-quality interpretation. Persistently weak entry rates and deteriorating wage progression would support a different explanation. Compare the JOLTS charts with household survey unemployment durations and worker-level transitions; the aggregate rates alone cannot distinguish these mechanisms.

questions.question: How much of the reported input-price pressure reaches consumer prices?
questions.detail: Use the two Fed staff studies Waller cites to identify high-tech and energy-sensitive categories, then compare the sequence of purchasing-manager reports, producer prices and PCE outcomes. Check whether observed movements persist after input prices turn. Evidence on timing can identify a near-term risk to a rates position, while the scale of the risk also depends on expenditure weights.
